sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities fell sharply as a Thursday AI and semiconductor rout, Wall Street's worst session since April 2025, dragged most markets lower before a Friday rebound limited losses. MSCI World slipped roughly **2%**, with MSCI Developed Markets broadly similar (approx., verify before merging), while MSCI Emerging Markets ended near **1,502**, down around **4%** (approx., verify before merging). The S&P 500 lost **2.7%** to **7,376.86**, and the mega-cap MAG7/tech cohort fell hardest, the Nasdaq 100 down about **6.4%** (approx., verify before merging). Europe held up better, the Euro Stoxx 50 near **6,170** and roughly flat on the week (approx., verify before merging). In Asia the Nikkei 225 crashed **9.25%** to **57,434.77**, while Chinese equities bucked the trend, the CSI 300 up **1.73%** and the Hang Seng up **5.10%**.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US stocks posted their worst week in months as AI-spending scepticism and soft semiconductor guidance triggered a Thursday sell-off, the steepest session since April 2025, that erased roughly **$3tn** in value and pushed the Nasdaq into correction. The S&P 500 fell **2.7%** to **7,376.86**, the Nasdaq Composite dropped **3.4%** to **24,579.42** for a fourth straight weekly loss, and the Dow eased about **0.9%**.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged more than **12%** at the week's lows, and the energy sector sank about **12%**, its worst week since April 2025, as crude tumbled. A Friday rebound, the Nasdaq up **1.1%**, followed a stronger-than-expected October payrolls print of **165,000** jobs against about **65,000** expected, with unemployment at **4.1%**.

Stretched mega-cap valuations, the prospect of tighter AI oversight and a Democratic sweep in the midterm elections framed the risk-off tone, even as resilient jobs data tempered recession fears and kept a December Fed move in play.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities proved relatively resilient, cushioned by lighter mega-cap tech exposure even as the global AI sell-off hit sentiment. The Euro Stoxx 50 closed around **6,170**, finishing the week roughly flat to marginally higher (approx., verify before merging), while the STOXX Europe 600 ended little changed; Friday brought broad declines, with the DAX down about **2%**.

AI-regulation worries and doubts over data-centre profitability weighed on technology and chip names, and energy shares slid alongside a near-**13%** collapse in crude. Weaker euro-area retail sales added to a soft macro backdrop, and reports that the ECB is reviewing bank lending tied to data centres underscored growing scrutiny of the AI investment cycle and left regional dispersion skewed against tech-heavy bourses.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian markets diverged sharply. Japan bore the brunt of the AI chip rout: the Nikkei 225 crashed **9.25%** to **57,434.77** and the TOPIX fell **6.48%**, tipping the Nikkei into a bear market more than **20%** below its June peak as mega-cap tech and semiconductor names led declines.

China bucked the global slide, with the CSI 300 up **1.73%** and the Hang Seng up **5.10%** on the week. The PBoC said it would raise its foreign-currency deposit reserve ratio from **4%** to **6%** from 15 November to temper yuan strength, a signal of policy support amid the regional turbulence.

South Korean equities tumbled, prompting regulators to temporarily ease margin-lending collateral rules to limit forced selling, highlighting the acute pressure on the region's tech-heavy indices.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar firmed as a stronger-than-expected October payrolls report revived expectations for a December Fed hike, with Convera framing the week around whether politics had popped the tech bubble. Safe-haven demand through the equity rout and widening rate differentials supported the greenback against most majors, with attention turning to upcoming US inflation data.

Sterling stayed relatively well supported, aided by its higher-yield appeal, while the euro traded cautiously against a firmer dollar and lingering French fiscal concerns. The yen remained under pressure amid Japan's equity collapse and a still-cautious BoJ, keeping USD/JPY elevated, while risk-sensitive EM currencies softened as capital sought safety.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Commodities suffered a broad sell-off that Saxo tied to an election shock, with precious metals the notable exception. Crude led the decline, Brent and WTI both shedding close to **13%**, their sharpest weekly drop in months, as markets priced a possible US-Iran de-escalation; Brent found support near its 200-day moving average around **$93.55** before recovering toward **$100**.

Copper fell **4.1%** as fading AI optimism and tariff uncertainty under a divided US Congress weighed on industrial metals. Gold held up best, cushioned by risk aversion despite some profit-taking after aggressive short-covering. The Bloomberg Commodity Index headed for a roughly **4%** weekly loss, its worst since April 2025, trimming its year-to-date gain to about **27%**.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Treasuries rallied during the equity rout before paring gains, leaving yields modestly changed on balance. The 10-year UST ended around **4.86%** and the 2-year near **4.51%**, dipping on Thursday's flight to safety then rising on Friday after firm payrolls, with curve moves driven by shifting Fed expectations and elevated oil-related inflation worries.

The Fed had held its target range at **3.75%-4.00%** in October on a 10-2 vote, with two dissents favouring a hike, and futures priced a December increase at roughly **78-85%** after the strong jobs print. IG credit held firm as a defensive haven, while HY spreads widened modestly amid the risk-off tone before stabilising into Friday's rebound.
